question: Why are high rate enhanced sedimentation units more sensitive to sudden flow increases than large conventional basins?
correctAnswer: Their smaller volume gives a much shorter detention time, so a surge quickly disturbs settled solids and floc
explanation: Compact high rate units trade volume for settling area; with little detention time in reserve, a hydraulic surge reaches the settling zone fast and can lift solids into the effluent.
options: Their tubes are built from weaker material than basin walls
They hold no sludge, so there is nothing to disturb
Their smaller volume gives a much shorter detention time, so a surge quickly disturbs settled solids and floc
They operate without any inlet structure at all
sourceTitle: US EPA: Surface Water Treatment Rules — supporting treatment resources
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Enhanced sedimentation performance. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Their tubes are built from weaker material than basin walls
optionB: They hold no sludge, so there is nothing to disturb
optionC: Their smaller volume gives a much shorter detention time, so a surge quickly disturbs settled solids and floc
optionD: They operate without any inlet structure at all

question: Which condition most supports good performance in a high rate settler?
correctAnswer: Even flow distribution and stable, well formed floc entering the unit
explanation: High rate settlers depend on uniform flow and on floc that arrives intact; surges and uneven distribution short circuit flow and carry floc over the weirs.
options: Even flow distribution and stable, well formed floc entering the unit
The highest possible inlet velocity the pumps can deliver
Frequent large swings in plant flow through the day
Warm sludge blankets held in the unit for several days
sourceTitle: WPI: 2025 Need-to-Know criteria
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Enhanced sedimentation performance. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Even flow distribution and stable, well formed floc entering the unit
optionB: The highest possible inlet velocity the pumps can deliver
optionC: Frequent large swings in plant flow through the day
optionD: Warm sludge blankets held in the unit for several days

question: In a solids contact clarifier, what is the purpose of maintaining a controlled sludge blanket?
correctAnswer: Rising water passes through the blanket, where incoming particles contact and are captured by the recirculating floc
explanation: A managed blanket of previously formed floc acts as a contact zone: new particles collide with and join the floc, which improves clarification beyond plain settling alone.
options: The blanket disinfects the water as it rises through it
The blanket adds alkalinity to replace what coagulation consumed
The blanket stops all flow so solids can settle for a full day
Rising water passes through the blanket, where incoming particles contact and are captured by the recirculating floc
sourceTitle: US EPA - Small Drinking Water Systems Handbook
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Enhanced sedimentation performance. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.

optionB: The blanket adds alkalinity to replace what coagulation consumed

question: In general, how does lowering the surface overflow rate on a clarifier affect solids removal?
correctAnswer: Removal improves because particles have more opportunity to settle before reaching the outlet
explanation: A lower overflow rate means the upward water velocity is smaller relative to particle settling velocity, so more particles are captured instead of carried out.
options: Removal worsens because the water moves too slowly to stay mixed
Removal improves because particles have more opportunity to settle before reaching the outlet
Removal is unchanged because overflow rate has no effect on settling
Removal improves only when the basin is taken out of service
sourceTitle: WPI: 2025 Need-to-Know criteria

question: Why do plate and tube settler surfaces need regular cleaning?
correctAnswer: Solids and growth on the surfaces can plug passages and upset flow distribution
explanation: Buildup narrows the passages between plates or tubes, which channels flow, raises local velocities, and washes settled solids out of the unit.
options: Cleaning restores the disinfectant residual in the basin
Solids and growth on the surfaces can plug passages and upset flow distribution
The plates dissolve slowly and must be polished to last
Cleaning changes the plate spacing to suit each season

question: A filter shows head loss rising much faster than normal during a run. What is the most likely cause?
correctAnswer: Solids are accumulating in and on the media faster than usual
explanation: Rapid head loss development usually means the bed is capturing more solids than normal or the surface is blinding, both of which restrict flow through the media.
options: The backwash troughs have been set too low
The raw water temperature has fallen overnight
The effluent valve is fully open
Solids are accumulating in and on the media faster than usual
sourceTitle: US EPA: Surface Water Treatment Rules — supporting treatment resources

question: During backwashing, filter media is seen washing over the troughs and going to drain. What is the most likely cause?
correctAnswer: The backwash rate is set too high, expanding the bed beyond its design limit so media carries over
explanation: Excessive backwash flow over expands the bed; once the expanded surface reaches the trough lips, media grains spill over and are lost to drain.
options: The backwash rate is set too high, expanding the bed beyond its design limit so media carries over
The air scour valve was left closed during the wash
The raw water turbidity was unusually low that day
The filter run before the wash was shorter than usual

question: Air binding in a gravity filter is best described as what?
correctAnswer: Air released from the water collects in the media and blocks flow passages
explanation: Water under negative head can release dissolved air inside the bed; the trapped bubbles occupy pore space, raise head loss, and shorten the run.
options: Air leaking into the clearwell through the roof hatch
Bubbles forming in the chlorine contact tank
Air released from the water collects in the media and blocks flow passages
Air used to scour the bed during backwash

question: Cracks appearing across the surface of a filter bed usually indicate what?
correctAnswer: The bed has shrunk and pulled away after inadequate cleaning and mudball buildup
explanation: Surface cracking is a classic sign of a dirty, compacted bed where accumulated solids cause the media mass to shrink and split as it dewaters.
options: The media has been replaced too recently
The filter is producing water that is too clear
The underdrain system is brand new
The bed has shrunk and pulled away after inadequate cleaning and mudball buildup

explanation: A mid run breakthrough with no other change often means water has found a low resistance path, such as a crack or a disturbed area, and is bypassing filtration.

Flow is channelling through the bed instead of passing evenly through the media
The raw water has become too soft
The clearwell level is too steady

explanation: Free chlorine combines with ammonia to form chloramines; the ammonia may occur naturally in the source or be fed deliberately ahead of the chlorine.

question: Why do operators control the chlorine to ammonia ratio and pH carefully in a chloraminated system?
correctAnswer: To favour monochloramine and limit the di and trichloramine forms that cause taste and odour complaints
explanation: Monochloramine is the desired disinfectant species; poor ratio or pH control shifts formation toward dichloramine and trichloramine, which have strong tastes and odours and weaker disinfection value.

To make the water harder so pipes last longer
To remove the need for any residual testing
To convert all ammonia instantly to nitrogen gas

question: Compared with a free chlorine residual, a chloramine residual is best described how?
correctAnswer: More stable and longer lasting, but a weaker disinfectant that needs longer contact time
explanation: Chloramines react more slowly, which lets the residual persist far into a distribution system, but that same stability means disinfection credit requires much longer contact time than free chlorine.
options: More stable and longer lasting, but a weaker disinfectant that needs longer contact time
Stronger acting and used up within minutes
Identical in strength but different in colour
Unable to be measured with standard test kits

question: A chloraminated system with excess free ammonia is at risk of nitrification. What happens during nitrification?
correctAnswer: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate, consuming the chloramine residual
explanation: Where free ammonia remains, nitrifying bacteria can grow in the distribution system, producing nitrite, destroying chloramine, and lowering pH and alkalinity as they spread.
options: Ammonia evaporates and leaves the water completely
Chloramine converts back to a strong free chlorine residual
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate, consuming the chloramine residual
Calcium precipitates and coats the pipe walls

question: A sample has phenolphthalein alkalinity P of 30 mg/L as CaCO3 and total alkalinity T of 100 mg/L as CaCO3. Because P is less than half of T, which pair gives its carbonate and bicarbonate alkalinity?
